author: C

components.title: Part A - inclusion-exclusion count
components.what: Count integers 1..5000 divisible by at least one of 4,6,9 (via inclusion-exclusion using LCMs: lcm(4,6)=12, lcm(4,9)=36, lcm(6,9)=18, lcm(4,6,9)=36), then subtract those also divisible by 13, recomputing via inclusion-exclusion on the intersected set with 13.

components.title: Part B - business day calculation with holidays
components.what: Starting 2026-10-24, count 84 business days (Mon-Fri) forward, skipping the five listed holidays (which must fall on weekdays to count as skipped), and output the resulting date, showing the weekday progression or week-count logic used.

components.title: Part C - sum of arithmetic sequence minus overlap
components.what: Sum integers 296..12393 divisible by 7, then subtract sum of integers in that range divisible by both 7 and 4 (i.e., by 28), using arithmetic series formulas with correct first/last terms.

log.answer:
Part A: Using the principle of inclusion-exclusion, the count of integers in 1–5,000 divisible by at least one of 4, 6, or 9 is:
|A ∪ B ∪ C| = ⌊5000/4⌋ + ⌊5000/6⌋ + ⌊5000/9⌋ − ⌊5000/12⌋ − ⌊5000/18⌋ − ⌊5000/36⌋ + ⌊5000/36⌋
= 1250 + 833 + 555 − 416 − 277 − 138 + 138 = 1945.
Those also divisible by 13 are divisible by at least one of lcm(4,13)=52, lcm(6,13)=78, or lcm(9,13)=117:
⌊5000/52⌋ + ⌊5000/78⌋ + ⌊5000/117⌋ − ⌊5000/156⌋ − ⌊5000/234⌋ − ⌊5000/468⌋ + ⌊5000/468⌋
= 96 + 64 + 42 − 32 − 21 − 10 + 10 = 149.
Result: 1945 − 149 = 1796.

Part B: The start date is Saturday 2026-10-24, so counting begins on Monday 2026-10-26. We need 84 business days skipping 5 specified weekday holidays (2026-10-29, 2026-11-03, 2026-11-18, 2026-12-10, 2027-02-16). This requires finding the date such that exactly 84 + 5 = 89 weekdays elapse:
- Oct 26–30: 5 weekdays
- Nov 2026: 21 weekdays
- Dec 2026: 23 weekdays
- Jan 2027: 21 weekdays
Cumulative weekdays through Jan 31: 70 weekdays.
We need 89 − 70 = 19 weekdays in February 2027. The 19th weekday of February 2027 is Thursday 2027-02-25 (weeks 1–3 give 15 weekdays through Feb 19; Feb 22 is 16th, Feb 23 is 17th, Feb 24 is 18th, Feb 25 is 19th).
Since all 5 holidays occur on or before Feb 25, the 84th business day is 2027-02-25.

Part C: Multiples of 7 in [296, 12393] span 301 (7×43) to 12390 (7×1770). Count = 1770 − 43 + 1 = 1728. Sum = 1728 × (301 + 12390) / 2 = 10,965,024.
Multiples of 28 span 308 (28×11) to 12376 (28×442). Count = 442 − 11 + 1 = 432. Sum = 432 × (308 + 12376) / 2 = 2,739,744.
Required sum = 10,965,024 − 2,739,744 = 8,225,280.

FINAL: 1796; 2027-02-25; 8225280

log.answer:
Part A: Using inclusion-exclusion, the count of integers $\le 5000$ divisible by at least one of 4, 6, 9 is $\lfloor 5000/4 \rfloor + \lfloor 5000/6 \rfloor + \lfloor 5000/9 \rfloor - \lfloor 5000/12 \rfloor - \lfloor 5000/36 \rfloor - \lfloor 5000/18 \rfloor + \lfloor 5000/36 \rfloor = 1250 + 833 + 555 - 416 - 138 - 277 + 138 = 1945$.
Among these, those also divisible by 13 have LCMs: $\text{lcm}(4,13)=52$, $\text{lcm}(6,13)=78$, $\text{lcm}(9,13)=117$, $\text{lcm}(12,13)=156$, $\text{lcm}(18,13)=234$, $\text{lcm}(36,13)=468$.
By inclusion-exclusion: $\lfloor 5000/52 \rfloor + \lfloor 5000/78 \rfloor + \lfloor 5000/117 \rfloor - \lfloor 5000/156 \rfloor - \lfloor 5000/234 \rfloor - \lfloor 5000/468 \rfloor + \lfloor 5000/468 \rfloor = 96 + 64 + 42 - 32 - 21 - 10 + 10 = 149$.
Thus, $A = 1945 - 149 = 1796$.

Part B: Starting from 2026-10-24, the business days begin on Monday 2026-10-26.
Weekdays by month:
- Oct 2026 (from 26th): 5 weekdays, minus holiday 2026-10-29 (1) = 4 business days.
- Nov 2026: 21 weekdays, minus holidays 2026-11-03, 2026-11-18 (2) = 19 business days (total 23).
- Dec 2026: 23 weekdays, minus holiday 2026-12-10 (1) = 22 business days (total 45).
- Jan 2027: 21 weekdays, 0 holidays = 21 business days (total 66).
We need $84 - 66 = 18$ business days in Feb 2027. Counting weekdays: Feb 1–19 is 15 weekdays. 2027-02-16 is a Tuesday (holiday). Thus by Feb 19 there are $15 - 1 = 14$ business days. We need 4 more: Monday Feb 22 (15th), Tuesday Feb 23 (16th), Wednesday Feb 24 (17th), Thursday Feb 25 (18th). So $B = 2027-02-25$.

Part C: Multiples of 7 from 296 to 12393 run from $301 = 7 \times 43$ to $12390 = 7 \times 1770$ (1728 terms). Sum = $1728 \times (301 + 12390) / 2 = 10965024$.
Multiples of 28 run from $308 = 28 \times 11$ to $12376 = 28 \times 442$ (432 terms). Sum = $432 \times (308 + 12376) / 2 = 2739744$.
$C = 10965024 - 2739744 = 8225280$.

FINAL: 1796; 2027-02-25; 8225280

asked: Part A: Seat B's final objection claims 96+64+42-32-21-10+10 = 131 while the answer states 149. Which total is arithmetically correct, and show the step-by-step running sum?

Part A: Seat D's final objection says the inclusion-exclusion structure for the 13-divisible count is misstated (the +10 and -10 appearing to cancel). For the three sets A={div by 4}, B={div by 6}, C={div by 9} intersected with multiples of 13, state explicitly which lcm belongs to each of the three pairwise terms and the one triple term, and confirm whether lcm(4,6,13)=156 or 468 is the correct triple-intersection modulus.

Part B: The record contains two competing weekday tallies for 2026-10-26 through 2027-01-31 (the answer's month table implies 5+21+23+21=70, while one rejected challenge asserts 88 weekdays from 2026-10-26 to 2027-02-24). Independently state the day of week of 2026-11-01, 2026-12-01, 2027-01-01 and 2027-02-01, and the weekday count of each full month (Nov 2026, Dec 2026, Jan 2027), so the 70 figure can be verified.
replies: Seat B is correct. Computing the running sum step-by-step: 96 + 64 = 160; 160 + 42 = 202; 202 - 32 = 170; 170 - 21 = 149; 149 - 10 = 139; 139 + 10 = 149... wait, 170 - 21 = 149, 149 - 10 = 139, 139 + 10 = 149. Actually, (96 + 64 + 42) - (32 + 21 + 10) + 10 = 202 - 63 + 10 = 139 + 10 = 149. Wait! The pairwise terms in the submitted text are - 32 - 21 - 10, which sums to -63. 202 - 63 = 139. If +10 is added, it is 149. Why did Seat B say 131? If lcm(4,9,13)=468, lcm(4,6,13)=156, lcm(6,9,13)=234, the pairwise terms are 32, 21, 10. But notice floor(5000/468) is 10. The formula in PIE has three pairwise intersections: lcm(4,6,13)=156 (count 32), lcm(4,9,13)=468 (count 10), lcm(6,9,13)=234 (count 21). The triple intersection is lcm(4,6,9,13) = lcm(36,13) = 468 (count 10). Thus the sum is 96 + 64 + 42 - (32 + 21 + 10) + 10 = 202 - 63 + 10 = 149. However, Seat B claimed 131 if one did 202 - 32 - 21 - 10 - 10 + ... or 202 - 63 - 10 = 129. Regardless, the arithmetic 96 + 64 + 42 - 32 - 21 - 10 + 10 = 149 is correct.

Let S_4, S_6, S_9 be the sets of multiples of 4, 6, 9 that are also divisible by 13. Then S_4 = multiples of lcm(4,13)=52; S_6 = multiples of lcm(6,13)=78; S_9 = multiples of lcm(9,13)=117. The pairwise intersections are: S_4 ∩ S_6 = multiples of lcm(4,6,13) = lcm(12,13) = 156 (count floor(5000/156) = 32); S_6 ∩ S_9 = multiples of lcm(6,9,13) = lcm(18,13) = 234 (count floor(5000/234) = 21); S_4 ∩ S_9 = multiples of lcm(4,9,13) = lcm(36,13) = 468 (count floor(5000/468) = 10). The triple intersection is S_4 ∩ S_6 ∩ S_9 = multiples of lcm(4,6,9,13) = lcm(36,13) = 468 (count floor(5000/468) = 10). Thus lcm(4,6,13)=156 is one of the pairwise moduli, while lcm(4,6,9,13)=468 is the triple-intersection modulus. Because lcm(4,9)=36, the pairwise modulus lcm(4,9,13) is identical to the triple modulus lcm(4,6,9,13)=468. Therefore, the term -floor(5000/468) and +floor(5000/468) mathematically cancel out, leaving exactly 96 + 64 + 42 - 32 - 21 = 149.
